title: F test of two variances
biology: Evolutionary developmental biologists compare variation in wing length between two inbred fly lines.
design: Thirty independent flies per line are reared under a common environment.
other_examples: Variation in enzyme activity across two treatments
question: Is wing-length variance the same in the two fly lines?
null: The population variance ratio (Line A / Line B) is 1.
assumptions: Highly sensitive to outliers and non-normality
parametric: If comparing means, use Welch without a variance pretest
Model group-specific variances when variability is the target
nonparametric: Brown–Forsythe is less sensitive to non-normality
Resample within groups for a variance-ratio interval

plot_args.note: Display the two distributions side by side
Give each group its own color

practice: Could the variance test detect a difference even when the two population means are identical?
code_simulate:
set.seed(1109)
d <- data.frame(line = rep(c("Line A", "Line B"), each = 30),
                wing_mm = c(rnorm(30, 2.6, .11), rnorm(30, 2.6, .21)))
write.csv(d, file.path(output_dir, "data.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
code_plot:
beeswarm(wing_mm ~ line, data = d, pch = 21,
         bg = c("#246A73", "#B7663E"), col = "white", cex = 1.3,
         xlab = "Fly line", ylab = "Wing length (mm)")
code_analysis:
d$line <- factor(d$line, levels = c("Line A", "Line B"))
fit <- var.test(wing_mm ~ line, data = d, ratio = 1,
                alternative = "two.sided", conf.level = .95)
generating_model: 30 wing lengths per independent fly line come from normal distributions with shared mean 2.6 mm, SD 0.11 for Line A and SD 0.21 for Line B.
generating_truth: Population means are equal, but the true variance ratio A/B is 0.11 squared / 0.21 squared, approximately 0.274.

columns.name: wing_mm
columns.meaning: Wing length of one independent fly

teaching_point: A variance question can have a different answer from a mean question; the exact F test depends strongly on normality.
